Ignatius is declared heavenly patron of all Spiritual Exercises and of every institute, sodality and group that serves those who make them. The constitution dates itself to the third centenary of his canonisation and the fourth of the 'golden booklet'.
glosses.quote: S. Ignatium de Loyola omnium Exercitiorum Spiritualium ideoque institutorum, sodalitiorum, coetuum cuiusvis generis, iis qui Exercitia Spiritualia obeunt, operam studiumque navantium, Patronum Caelestem declaramus, constituimus, renuntiamus.

glosses.note: Among all methods of retreat one has always held first place: that of Ignatius, 'chief and particular master of the Spiritual Exercises'. The encyclical quotes Pius XI's own words from before his election calling the book a code of norms 'wholly universal'.
glosses.quote: methodum intelligimus invectam a sancto Ignatio de Loyola, quem praecipuum et peculiarem Magistrum Exercitiorum spiritualium appellare placet

glosses.note: Among the book's excellences the encyclical names its 'admirable ease' of adaptation to every order and state of life, contemplatives and people in secular business alike: the theme of the last three Annotations. In the same sentence the doctrine is called free of the dangers of 'false mysticism', a phrase that belongs to the ascetical–mystical debate of the 1920s.
glosses.quote: admirabilis facilitas Exercitia haec ad quemvis hominum ordinem ac statum accommodandi, sive ii in coenobiis contemplationi incumbunt, sive in saecularibus negotiis actuosam vitam traducunt

glosses.note: The rector announces a three-day school retreat in honour of Francis Xavier; the preacher defines a retreat as withdrawal from ordinary cares for self-examination, the separation the twentieth Annotation asks of the one who makes the Exercises.
glosses.quote: A retreat, my dear boys, signifies a withdrawal for a while from the cares of our life, the cares of this workaday world, in order to examine the state of our conscience, to reflect on the mysteries of holy religion and to understand better why we are here in this world.

glosses.note: The retreat is preached on the four last things, beginning with death and judgment. Ignatius names death and judgment in the sixth Addition as what to keep before oneself in the First Week; the retreat tradition turned them into sermons of their own.
glosses.quote: During these few days I intend to put before you some thoughts concerning the four last things. They are, as you know from your catechism, death, judgment, hell and heaven.

glosses.note: The two hell sermons follow the fifth exercise of the First Week through the five senses, sight, smell, hearing, taste and touch, and then through the 'worm of conscience' that Ignatius puts under taste. Joyce's reader receives the meditation as rhetoric aimed at a boy.
glosses.quote: Every sense of the flesh is tortured and every faculty of the soul therewith: the eyes with impenetrable utter darkness, the nose with noisome odours, the ears with yells and howls and execrations, the taste with foul matter, leprous corruption, nameless suffocating filth, the touch with redhot goads and spikes, with cruel tongues of flame.

glosses.note: The preacher names the method he has been using: the composition of place, with Ignatius as 'our holy founder'. The one explicit reference to the book in the novel.
glosses.quote: This morning we endeavoured, in our reflection upon hell, to make what our holy founder calls in his book of spiritual exercises, the composition of place.

glosses.title: El Reino de Dios y el Reino de Cristo, o el Evangelio y los Ejercicios de San Ignacio
glosses.note: The Kingdom of God of the Gospels set beside the call of the King: the Kingdom of Christ as 'cipher and key' of the Exercises, which are a practice of the Gospel as the Gospel is the Kingdom of God.

glosses.author: Arturo Codina
glosses.title: ¿La meditación de «Dos Banderas» es de San Ignacio o de un anónimo?
glosses.note: Taking up Van Ortroy's article in the Analecta Bollandiana (1913) and the thesis that Ignatius took the Two Standards from the pseudo-Bernardine parable De conflictu vitiorum et virtutum read at Loyola. The author is named from his own reference in the sequel.

glosses.author: Arturo Codina
glosses.title: ¿En Manresa o en París?
glosses.note: Sequel: Tournier's thesis (Études, 1910) that the Two Standards depends on Werner of St Blasien's De duobus dominis and on Augustine, and the question whether the meditation was made at Manresa or in Paris; the second part reads its fruit with Meschler and Suárez as perfection in any state, not a call to apostolic life.

glosses.author: Antonio Astrain
glosses.title: San Ignacio de Loyola y la Liturgia
glosses.note: The historian of the Spanish Jesuits answers Dom Festugière's La Liturgie catholique (1913) in three articles: Ignatius' own practice of the liturgy, the charge of individualism, and the 'spirit and method' of the Exercises.

glosses.author: Arturo Codina
glosses.title: Los «Ejercicios» de San Ignacio y el «Ejercitatorio» de Cisneros
glosses.note: Against Dom Besse and Dom Pierdet of Silos (Revista Eclesiástica, 1916–17), who derived the Exercises from García de Cisneros' Ejercitatorio (Montserrat, 1500): the claimed parallels are weighed one by one; that Ignatius read the Ejercitatorio is granted as probable, a dependence of the book is not proven.

glosses.author: Arturo Codina
glosses.title: Los «Ejercicios» de San Ignacio y el «Ejercitatorio» de Cisneros (conclusion)
glosses.note: The composition of place and the examen after prayer are struck from the list of borrowings: they are not in the Ejercitatorio but in Cisneros' separate Directorio de las horas canónicas.

glosses.author: F. de Manresa
glosses.title: Suárez, asceta: Suárez y el libro de los «Ejercicios»
glosses.note: Suárez's defence of the Exercises in De religione Societatis Iesu, book IX, presented as the theology of a rough stone from the quarry of Manresa: an instrument of perfection, universal and safe.

glosses.author: José M. Bover
glosses.title: El «Principio y Fundamento» de los «Ejercicios» a la luz de las Epístolas de San Pablo
glosses.note: The Foundation read through Paul: the source from which all the Exercises flow and on which they rest, and the paradox that, giving and bearing everything, it does not of itself finish anything.
The annotations: later than Manresa; their origin and the corrections in the autograph; compared with Ludolph's Vita Christi.
The Foundation dated to Manresa; its antecedents in Ludolph's Vita Christi and in the Imitation of Christ.
The particular examen: whether it dates from Manresa; examens in Mauburnus; it did not always stand at the head of the book.
How the general examen is made.
The meditation on hell founded on Scripture; the tenderness of its petition; its text compared with Cisneros'.
The additions: their origin and meaning.
The Kingdom dated to Manresa; an autograph correction; the text of its second part; Anselm on the kingdom of Christ among its antecedents.
The Two Standards as part of the method of election; exposition; the example of Christ; the text compared with Ludolph.
The Three Classes: their end, their link with Annotation 16, their origin.
The three kinds of humility: the third, and the foundation of all three.
The election: its place in the book, its date (Manresa), its last preparation.
The rules for eating: their origin, with Brettle's view of it.
The Contemplation to Attain Love: origin.
The three methods of prayer: origin.
The rules for discernment: origin; the remedies for desolation.
The rules for alms: origin and their link with Manresa.
The rules for thinking with the Church: origin, an autograph correction, the Church as mother.
Cisneros' own summary of his Ejercitatorio and its chapter list, then Dom Besse's parallels examined (pp. 265–281): the question of the author's articles in Razón y Fe (1917) taken up again.
Fascicle 3: the annotations, translated, as introduction.
Day 1, exercises I–III: three considerations on the Foundation, the third on indifference before every election.
Day 2, exercise IV: the threefold sin.
Exercise V: one's own sins, followed by an added meditation on venial sins.
Exercise VII: hell. Day 3 adds death, the particular judgment and 'perfect conversion', for which the book leaves room in [71].
Exercises XI–XII: the Kingdom of Jesus Christ and its repetition, on the evening of day 3.
Day 4: contemplation I joins the Incarnation and the Nativity, as Torti says he joins exercises the book keeps apart; then the Presentation, the flight into Egypt and the hidden life.
Exercise XVI: application of the senses to the mysteries of the day.
Day 5, exercises XVII–XVIII: the Two Standards and its repetition.
Exercise XIX: the three classes of men.
Exercise XX: the three degrees of humility, 'the sum of Christian perfection'.
Day 7: four contemplations of the Passion, ending in a summary of the whole Passion.
Day 8: the Resurrection and the apparition to Our Lady, the appearances, the Ascension.
Exercise XXXII: 'divine love stirs in us a love without measure', the Contemplation to Attain Love.
Fascicle 43, § 1: rules for discernment, with a 'historical counterpart' (pp. 414–423): the conversion of the poet Adolphe Retté (1906), told as a living instance of the rules.
§ 2: scruples and 'two kindred serpentine persuasions'.
§ 3: on making a sound election, opening with a Latin text.
Translation of the rules for alms and for 'thinking sincerely with the Catholic Church'.

The ego depends on something greater and is directed towards it as its goal; Jung hears this in the opening sentence of the Foundation, which his note gives in Latin, with a reference to Rickaby, p. 18.
glosses.linkLabel: CW 9ii in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.note: 'Homo creatus est' as the fundamentum of the Exercises: the self precedes the ego, which does not make itself. Jung calls this half of the psychological truth; the other half is that man also shapes what made him.

glosses.note: The colloquy as a technique of inner dialogue, admitted by Ignatius with one restriction: only the meditant speaks, and the answers from within are set aside as merely human. The note cites Izquierdo (1686) on the colloquy as familiar talk with Christ. Not everyone, Jung adds, is fit for such exercises.
glosses.linkLabel: CW 9i in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.note: Ruland's alchemical definition of meditatio as inner dialogue with an unseen other; Jung's note finds it very close to the colloquy of the Exercises.
glosses.linkLabel: CW 12 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.note: Exercitia spiritualia and yoga as techniques of transformation: methods fixed in advance to bring about a definite psychic effect. Placed on Annotation 1, the book's own definition of spiritual exercises (editorial).
glosses.linkLabel: CW 9i in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.loc: CW 13 (Paracelsus as a Spiritual Phenomenon), §201, note
glosses.note: Paracelsus' 'imitation' of Aniadus by imagination compared with active imagination in the Exercises: consideratio, contemplatio, meditatio, ponderatio and imaginatio per sensus serve the 'realization' of what is imagined. The note sends the reader to Rickaby, pp. 40ff., the meditation on hell, and compares the contemplation of the life of Jesus.
glosses.linkLabel: CW 13 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.note: The bitterness of the sea and of damnation: the fourth point of the fifth exercise, tasting bitter things in hell, cited from Rickaby, p. 41, beside the more lurid hell exercise of the Jesuit Sebastián Izquierdo (1686).
glosses.linkLabel: CW 14 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.note: Imagination through the five senses (Rickaby, p. 41, the hell meditation) as the fullest possible 'realization' of the object of contemplation, which Jung sets beside the alchemist's total act of recognition.
glosses.linkLabel: CW 14 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.note: Imitating Christ 'by use of his senses', from the first method of prayer (Rickaby, p. 215): the same argument as the previous gloss.
glosses.linkLabel: CW 14 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.loc: CW 11 (Commentary on The Tibetan Book of the Great Liberation), §793
glosses.note: Ignatius used active imagination, Jung's own term for his method, in the Exercises. Jung names no paragraph; placed on the composition of place, seeing with the eye of the imagination (editorial).
glosses.linkLabel: CW 11 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.note: The Christian contemplative of the Exercises grasps the holy image as concretely as possible, with all the senses, as the yogi solidifies what he contemplates. Placed on the application of the senses (editorial).
glosses.linkLabel: CW 11 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.note: Exercises and yoga alike give the meditant an object and so shut out his own fantasies as worthless; the West, apart from the very limited use of the Jesuit Exercitia, has developed nothing like yoga, out of fear of the personal unconscious.
glosses.linkLabel: CW 11 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.note: Like Shri Ramana's extinction of the ego in the self, the Exercitia subordinate self-possession to possession by Christ. Placed on the Suscipe (editorial).
glosses.linkLabel: CW 11 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.note: Recalling his ETH course on the Exercitia, Jung speaks of the total surrender they ask for, in which one never knows whether one meets sanctity or spiritual pride. Placed on the Suscipe (editorial).
glosses.linkLabel: CW 18 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.note: Is the Christ to whom one surrenders the Christ of the Synoptics, of the Exercitia, of a monk of Athos, of Zinzendorf? The Christ of the Exercises as one image among many.
glosses.linkLabel: CW 18 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.loc: CW 8 (On the Nature of the Psyche), §395
glosses.note: From the Autobiography, not the Exercises: the bright serpent-like light full of eyes that first consoled Ignatius and was later recognized as an evil spirit, read by Jung as an image of the many luminosities of the unconscious. Placed on the rules for the enemy who comes as an angel of light (editorial).
glosses.linkLabel: CW 8 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.loc: CW 7 (On the Psychology of the Unconscious), §119
glosses.note: The serpent vision, taken first for a divine and then for a diabolical visitation, as an instance of an original experience replaced by borrowed interpretation. Placed on the rules for the second week's discernment (editorial).
glosses.linkLabel: CW 7 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.note: The serpent vision as a humanly limited interpretation of an experience, with 1 John 4:1 on testing the spirits. Placed on the second week's rules of discernment (editorial).
glosses.linkLabel: CW 11 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.note: Nothing guarantees that the spirit is not the devil, as with Ignatius' serpens oculatus, taken first for Christ and later for the devil. Placed on the second week's rules of discernment (editorial).
glosses.linkLabel: CW 18 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.note: As the struggle of light and darkness moved inward, Ignatius thought it necessary to make the conflict felt through drastic exercises. The note cites Rickaby, pp. 75ff., which are Rickaby's notes on the later rules of discernment for the first week, the enemy's tactics.
glosses.linkLabel: CW 13 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.note: Jung ascribes to Ignatius the maxim that the end sanctifies the means, drawn from the authority of the Church, and sets it beside the Marxist state. The maxim is not in the Exercises; placed on the thirteenth rule for thinking with the Church (editorial).
glosses.linkLabel: CW 10 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.note: Meditation today: a theme chosen by the meditant or set by an instructor, as in the Ignatian Exercitia; of value for concentration, not for an encounter with the unconscious. Placed on Annotation 2, on the one who gives the matter (editorial).
glosses.linkLabel: CW 14 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.note: The Exercitia as the Western parallel to yoga: both impress fixed forms, here fixed ideas of salvation, on consciousness, which is right as long as the symbol still expresses the unconscious situation.
glosses.linkLabel: CW 12 in the Collected Works apparatus

glosses.author: Ivo Zeiger

glosses.loc: Zeitschrift für Aszese und Mystik 17 (1942), pp. 1–16 · Abhandlungen
glosses.note: Written in Rome by a canon lawyer: the parable of the King [91]-[100] explained by medieval legal history as Germanic 'Gefolgschaft', in the vocabulary of the time ('Führereid', 'germanisch') and with v. Schwerin's Germanische Rechtsgeschichte (1936) among its sources. Its conclusions run the other way: following Christ means free choice, mutual loyalty and friendship, 'Freiheit, nicht Zwang', and is far removed from drill and soldiery. In the archive's PDF the article is followed by a printed appeal for the wartime Winterhilfswerk.

glosses.loc: Zeitschrift für Aszese und Mystik 12 (1937), pp. 172–177 · Abhandlungen
glosses.note: The agere contra of [97] defended against the charge of hostility to life through a 'heroic' image of man: loyalty, the 'Reichsgedanke Christi', readiness for battle. The decisive offering, Schuster insists, is not forced or commanded but given in free love.

glosses.author: Karl Rahner
glosses.title: Die ignatianische Mystik der Weltfreudigkeit
glosses.loc: Zeitschrift für Aszese und Mystik 12 (1937), pp. 121–137 · Abhandlungen
glosses.note: A lecture given in Vienna. Ignatian 'Weltfreudigkeit' is no naive optimism; it grows out of a mysticism of the cross and of indifference that seeks God alone and therefore finds him everywhere, 'in actione contemplativus'. The close turns to the present: the cross in personal life and 'im Geschick unseres Volkes', when it looks as if evening were falling over the West.

glosses.title: Die Maior Dei Gloria im Exerzitienbuch des hl. Ignatius
glosses.loc: Zeitschrift für Aszese und Mystik 9 (1934), pp. 337–348 · Abhandlungen
glosses.note: The 'maior Dei gloria' read through the biblical doxa, from Exodus and Ezekiel to John and Paul. The 'more' at the end of the Foundation and the Contemplation to Attain Love lead to the border of asceticism and mysticism, where the doxa is the 'Durchbruchstelle'. Placed on the Foundation (editorial).

glosses.loc: Zeitschrift für Aszese und Mystik 8 (1933), pp. 211–229 · Abhandlungen
glosses.note: Three years later the same author's vocabulary has changed. Christ is 'Haupt und Führer', owed 'treueste Gefolgschaft'; the kingdom of the parable is the Catholic world Church 'im Kampf der Zeit', and Catholic Action grows 'organisch' out of the meditation. Neither the state nor the party is named.

glosses.title: Die Ignatianische Gebetsweise. Aus dem Nachlasse des P. Anton Huonder S.J.

glosses.author: Hubert Kroppenberg
glosses.title: Nochmals: Geschichtliches zur Königsbetrachtung des hl. Ignatius
glosses.loc: Zeitschrift für Aszese und Mystik 7 (1932), pp. 364–366 · Kleine Beiträge
glosses.note: A reply to Kellerwessel. The Spanish nobleman's duty to follow his king to war explains the 'oblationes majoris aestimationis' of [97]. In 'unserer demokratischen Zeit' the parable is hard to give: the retreat-giver may be taken for a disguised recruiter for political monarchy, and women retreatants find the soldier less near than the bride. Yet most people, the young above all, are 'Monarchisten' at heart, and the king of their heart may be called 'Hitler, Lenin oder Johann Wolfgang von Goethe'. Nostitz-Rieneck is quoted: today Ignatius might speak of a great social leader who carries the masses with him.

glosses.note: What did the parable owe to books, and what to its time? Literary antecedents (Basil, Anselm, Werner, John Climacus' call to a spiritual 'Gefolgschaft', scattered places in Ludolph, and after Leturia 1928 the prologue of the Flos Sanctorum) give suggestions at most; the parable is Ignatius' own. Stronger is the living ideal of his years: the crusade, the fall of Granada, Leo X's crusade plan of 1518, taken from an article by Hungerford Pollen in the Woodstock Letters (1916). The present, 'die Zeit des Christkönigsfestes und der Katholischen Aktion', needs above all the second part.
